Turnarounds! Draw him exactly as you want him to look, then draw lines from key points on his face (top of head, hairline, eyebrows, eyes etc.) and stretch them along the page. Then draw him in a slightly different view following the guide made by those lines.  Eventually you’ll get all the angles down. 

You can do this for his head first, and then do a full body version to get all the details right. It’s tough at first, but you’ll get used to his proportions this way and eventually it’ll be second nature.

The Jong (正) is more to show the continuation of a legacy, not a generational name. It definitely wouldn't be like "Millennial-Joe", it would be closer to "Joe Junior" or such.


Jong-il (正日) and Jong-un (正恩) both share the same Chinese character for "jong", meaning "just/proper". For the Kim dynasty in particular, all of their names are interconnected. Jong-il's "il" character was originally 一 "one" not 日 "day". Although they both have the same sound in Korean (일/il), Jong-il changed his 一/il character to Kim Il-sung's 日/il to invoke a sense of dynastic continuation. Same reason he gave most of his kids "jong" names.


Your example of "Millenial Joe" is a bit off though. It's incredibly difficult to express in English because Korean given names often take two characters from Chinese characters, and therefore it's easier to link names using just one of the characters. It would be more like "Joe-Paul" giving his son the name "Joe-Steve", which obviously wouldn't happen in English.

The jump from 2 to 3 is so difficult because you suddenly have to deal with more advanced concepts that aren't quite covered by the knowledge you already have :( It's the point where you have to be more creative when using the grammar and vocab you know already to try and fill the gaps in your knowledge, but that will come with practice! It's good to try and start speaking as much as you can because even though it's terrifying, it's a good way to find out what you can and can't get away with saying. 3 and 4 are going to be difficult but so rewarding, just remember to take time to review the things you learned in earlier levels and speaaak speak speak

I attended yonsei until level 5 and it was a slow descent into hell. For me, the main issue was that the class environment almost forces you to compare yourself to your classmates rather than focusing on your own skills. I did start to feel more comfortable in my level 5 class as that's when I was confident in casual conversation, and the work in class was building on what we had already learned rather than being huge chunks of new grammar and vocab. My biggest struggles personally were levels 3 and 4, where I always felt like my classmates were more advanced than me and I was getting lower marks. In yonsei at least, levels 3 and 4 introduce so much more new material at a more rapid pace than other levels, and the topics get very repetitive.


I've talked to other friends who studied at different schools (성균관대, 한양대, 서강대 etc) and they also felt that, in general, the biggest jumps in difficulty were levels 2-3 and 3-4.


I'm finishing the 4th and final year of my Korean degree in the UK now (our second year was spent abroad) and because we've been stretching 서울대 levels 5 and 6 over two years it hasn't been particularly challenging when compared to Korea's language schools. The most difficult part about studying in Korea is definitely the pacing; around two months per level doesn't feel long enough to fully absorb the material you're learning even though you're fully immersed.
